Author: @craigcampbell8560
Content: There's a lot of reasons, and corporate greed is ONLY one of them.  Like it or not, the UAW is a big part of the problem.  When an assembly line worker gets paid a LOT more to install the same parts (which in most cases doesn't require a ton of skill)  than the ASE certified mechanic that has diagnose and repair EVERY problem on EVERY vehicle (which takes a LOT more skill) there's a problem.  I'm NOT opposed to assembly line workers making good money, but how do you justify them making a lot more than a mechanic when their job IS easier in most cases and definitely required a lot less skill?  The UAW however, is nowhere near as big of a problem as the government is.  Government mandates and regulations have made ALL cars worse, including Japanese cars, even though the Japanese manufacturers have declined significantly less.  While a lot of mandated equipment DOES make cars safer, and in some cases, better, they ALL add cost, which is an issue because the massive cost of new vehicles these days is a problem.  This forces the manufacturers to cut costs and corners that they actually would prefer not to.  The worst is the CAFE standards.  How does one of the best and most reliable engines of all time become an unreliable piece of shit?  Adding a bunch of systems to it to keep it incompliance with increasingly stringent CAFE and emissions standards.  As if that's not bad enough, the larger and under stressed engines that were VERY reliable have been regulated out of existence by the government and replaced by tiny, overstressed engines that are as fragile as an egg.  While stricter emissions and standards and mileage requirements have proven to be good things in the past, they reached the point where they mandated unreliable garbage about 10 years ago.  While the Big 3 automakers have historically been terrible at coping with government regulations (Malaise era anyone?) it has reached the point where even Honda has had reliability issues, albeit considerably fewer and less severe than the big 3, because of modern CAFE and emissions standards, and Hondas have consistently been the most reliable for decades.  Add ALL of this together and there's little wonder than modern cars have become terrible.

Author: @alexanderSydneyOz
Content:
This is an excellent summary of this complex issues. 
I would like to clarify one part of it as many people seem to be under a staggering misunderstanding. 
Gm and Chrysler were not "bailed out". They were not given money. 
Rather, GM and Chrysler went bankrupt and the existing shareholders lost everything. At the end of the week he called me and told me it was ready.  When I picked it up he told me this was the first Mazda he had worked on and now knew why Japan was killing Detroit.  He told me "Your car has no head gasket. The top and block are so precisely machined there is no need for a gasket - we just ordered a new top as it was cracked.  The block was fine. Author: @paulsmith5611
Content: A small correction: After the gas crisis in the 1970s domestic auto makers DID try to get into small cars and compete with Japan. Chevy had the Chevette, Dodge had the Omni, Plymouth had the Horizon and Arrow (which was made by Mitsubishi), AMC had the Gremlin and Pacer, Ford had the Escort and Pinto. The problem is that Honda and Toyota just had a better product that was more reliable. Datsun as well to a point. The overhead cam engine was more efficient than an OHV engine for starters. This trend continued into the late 1990-early 2000s which in my opinion (as a long time automotive tech) was peak  automotive technology in terms of comfort and reliability. The Japanese 4 cylinder front wheel drive cars just couldn't be made much better, certainly not by the big three (edit: A timing chain, not a timing belt would have been better IMO and now that most have gone to chains I agree even more). Also, their small SUVs were as good as the cars, usually.  And vehicles have gone downhill in reliability ever sense, IMO. Then you add in Kia and Hyundai who have made some very good vehicles over the years (as well as some big failures) and the three domestics just realized they can't compete in the small car market. Lost in that decision are the few great full size cars that the domestics made, namely the Buick LaSabre/Regal V6 and the Ford Crown Victoria. I wish those two had stayed around. The Buick LaSabre may have had transmission issues though, some GM front wheel drive cars did have trans issues in the early and mid 2000s, I don't remember if Buick was one of them.

Author: @matttelo
Content:
It’s utterly tragic watching the same tired pattern play out again and again and again... This video tackles effectively yet another chapter in the ongoing American corporate tragedy.

The story of the Big Three isn’t just about cars. It’s a microcosm of what’s been happening across American industry for decades: Apple's demise in the 90s (before its Jobs-led revival) and again in the 2010's, Boeing post-mergers, the decimation of the steel industry, Harley-Davidson’s stagnation, even ENRON in its own way. The cycle is painfully familiar:

Innovation sparks a golden age:
America invents the product: cars, semiconductors, the personal computer, the airplane. And briefly becomes the undisputed global leader.

Finance and Wall Street move in:
The suits replace the engineers. Suddenly the mission isn’t building great products, it's juicing short-term stock prices and feeding shareholder returns.

Decline masked by marketing and loopholes:
As shown in the video, the Big Three abandoned sedans not because Americans didn’t want good cars, but because SUVs were more profitable thanks to legal loopholes and tariffs. They created artificial demand, cut corners, and buried quality to pad margins. Reliability rankings and recall stats tell the rest of the story.

Collapse becomes inevitable:
By the time the cracks are visible: layoffs, closures, bailouts.. It’s already too late. Taxpayers foot the bill while executives parachute out with bonuses.

The real heartbreak is that most of these innovations started here. The Model T, the microchip, the internet, even electric vehicles.. All pioneered in the US. But again and again, we see the same self-inflicted wound: corporate greed suffocates innovation. Long-term vision is replaced by quarterly earnings calls.

And what’s worse? The illusion of competition. Consumers are denied better foreign products due to protectionism like the “chicken tax,” while being told domestic options are brilliant in every sense. In reality, the average American pays more for lower-quality vehicles, and often can’t even access the best options from global manufacturers.

Meanwhile, upstarts like Tesla and Rivian succeed not because the US auto industry is "thriving", but because they avoided the legacy rot altogether. They were born in a new era. But how long before they, too, fall into the same trap?

This video is a wake-up call, not just about cars, but about a system that keeps sacrificing innovation, workers, and consumers at the altar of shareholder value. If we don’t break the cycle, the next industry to collapse might be something that destroys the whole American way of life.

Author: @qtdcanada
Content:
A correction is needed: the video said that Toyota, Honda and other Japanese carmakers don't have unions @ 3:09. This is wrong! 
Autoworkers in Japan, whether working for Toyota, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, etc. all belong to the JAW (Confederation of Japan Automobile Workers' Unions). The difference between Detroit Big 3 and UAW on one hand, and Japanese carmakers and JAW on the other hand, is that the Japanese business practice historically and still today emphasizes cooperation between the 2 sides; there is a belief in both sides that a strike will be bad for both of them, and it is best to resolve differences through gives-and-takes negotiation. This mentality is opposite to the American mentality of winner-takes-all, prevalent in both the Big-3 management and UAW. Also, another (big) difference is that Japan has universal health care, so Japanese carmakers do NOT carry an extra burden of funding health care for their workers, as is the situation with the Detroit Big 3 in dealing with UAW. 
The 'Light Truck' loophole that the Detroit Big 3 have relied on to survive will soon disappear, as Japanese (and European and South Korean) carmakers bring their SUVs to the market. After all, most consumers will choose a well-made, reliable 'light truck' (or SUV, whatever it is called) even if it carries a Japanese brand over an American-brand one prone to break down, expensive to fix.

Author: @miltonbrewster
Content:
Inadequate coverage of the problem.  

Detroit ran aground when it noticed that it made higher profits from FINANCING cars, than it made from BUILDING cars. That happened in the 1970s.  All three companies started promoting executives with accounting backgrounds, and ignoring executives with engineering backgrounds.  

As a consequence, Detroit stopped updating their manufacturing plants, but still had to compete with Japanese companies with new, updated, efficient manufacturing plant.

In 2010, the US Government had to bail out all three Detroit auto manufacturers. At that time, Obama had a golden opportunity to demand that Detroit upgrade its manufacturing plants, design and build more useful, robust vehicles,  and treat employees and consumers as well as it was treating Wall Street. Instead, Obama looked the other way, and Detroit continued its old ways, after paying off Government loans. 

There are many other problems, but these are the big two that this video didn't cover. 

Runner-up is Labor.  Only seven percent of a new car's wholesale price goes to labor -- this is the same for Japanese manufacturers as well.  Note that the BEST auto manufacturers in the world spends about as much on labor   as Detroit spends on Labor, and many overseas manufacturers actually spend more on Labor than we do.  American labor is not the problem here -- the American financial system IS.

Content: Starting at 2:16, you make inaccurate and misleading remarks regarding fuel efficiency efforts by American carmakers. Starting around 1977, most American carmakers began "downsizing" their full-size and mid-size passenger cars and making many efforts to improve fuel efficiency. In short order, American carmakers launched various fuel-efficient small and compact sedans such as the Chevrolet Citation, Ford Escort/Mercury Lynx, Dodge Omni/Plymouth Horizon, and K-car Dodge Aries/Plymouth Horizon. Whilst these "fuel saving" made-in-America cars sold in quite large numbers initially, quality control and reliability fell well short of Japanese small cars and in the case of the Citation there were an embarrassing number of safety recalls. During that time, some US "fuel saving" designs such as the General Motors V8-6-4 engine and the GM Diesel engine turned out to be dreadfully unreliable -- the term "lemon" doesn't even capture the essence of how bad these engines were. The "Big Three" rushed out to market "fuel efficient" vehicle designs without adequate stress testing, and the Detroit carmakers increasingly cut corners to save a few pennies here, a few pennies there. The Detroit carmakers began their most serious decline during this period -- even though they were making enormous efforts to produce fuel-efficient and safer cars -- because they faced serious price competition and quality-control competition from Japanese imports, while Detroit was saddled with very high labor overhead arising from overly-generous union contracts along with the need to compete on price with Japanese makers. The consumer demand for big trucks and SUVs didn't take place until the late '80s and '90s when fuel prices dropped from the Oil Embargo era, and this was due to consumer preference, NOT governmental regulators encouraging production of huge "gas guzzlers".

Content:
You talk as if unions are necessarily a bad thing. Well, every car manufacturer in every developed nation in the world, particularly Germany and Japan, has had strong unions for at least the last 80 years and none of them have the problems of American manufacturers.

Why is this? The answer lies in the fact that post-WWII the "West" other than the US, i.e., Europe, Japan, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and more recently South Korea, developed as mixed economies. That is to say, social democracies where strong economic development born out of post-war reconstruction was accompanied by the creation of a strong welfare state. America approved of this because it stopped Western Europe from "going communist."

However, this never occurred in America itself because not only had the US suffered no destruction during the war, hence no need for reconstruction, but it had emerged vastly richer because of it. The irony in this situation being that the Roosevelt administration's Social Security Act of 1935 had pioneered the welfare state in the first place at a time of widespread poverty and social distress. (It could also be pointed out that unregulated capitalism created the Great Depression that tanked the economy and it took enormous government spending during the war to rehabilitate it. Wall Street certainly didn't do anything to unf*ck the country.)

Under the welfare state system, crucial services such as healthcare and old age pensions are supplied by government to all citizens, rich or poor, old or young, regardless of income or lack thereof, and are funded by contributions paid in part by workers, in part by employers, and in part by general taxation. In the US on the other hand, where everything is for profit, healthcare is provided strictly to those who can afford it and health insurance is run by private companies whose focus is entirely on maximizing shareholder return by stiffing the policyholders at every turn with ever more far-fetched excuses.

Going back to Detroit's Big Three, back in the Seventies when multi-year collective bargaining agreements were negotiated between the employers and the UAW, in order to postpone labour cost increases as far into the future as possible, GM and co negotiated lower wage increases in exchange for the commitment to pay retirees 80% of their wage.

Needless to say, as the decades have rolled by and as the number of retired Detroit auto workers has not only increased but grown to outnumber the active workers, so the companies have found themselves deeper and deeper in a hole. Nonetheless, this is not only the self-inflicted consequence of decisions made by employers over fifty years ago, but also the natural consequence of putting the burden of providing public welfare services on private employers.

Author: @flxjhnlrssn
Content:
Regarding not being able to compete "because of unions", the unions in Sweden has a saying, something along these lines: "If your company can't afford to pay decent wages, your company deserves to fail". Assuming the problem is the wages is an extremely anti-labour stance. Obviously both the american car makers and unions are in a very different position to where Swedish businesses and unions are, and especially were they used to be. The american government does not provide the necessary business environment to allow "bad companies" to fail without seriously hurting the workers, you go into this in the video, but this is why unions need to back up the failing companies (unlike in Sweden, back in the day at least), it's because the government does not provide an alternative for them. But the american government also does not appear to provide a suitable environment for domestic car manufacturers to be able to increase productivity enough to justify "american wages", so clearly they deserve to "fail", afaik there is also a fairly large productivity gap between japanese and american auto makers, not just wages (if wages are even that different these days?). Anyway, blaming the american workers for demanding decent wages is hardly fair, and is practically taking a strong political stance against unionization in general, as especially in an economy like the US, the primary role of the unions is to safeguard the lives of their workers, keeping wages high enough being probably the most important aspect of that. You could just as well have blamed japanese auto workers/the japanese state for not unionizing/stopping unionization. Or more reasonably, you could blame the american government, or the whole global trade/financial system for creating these conditions where basic manufacturing jobs are forced to move to places with the lowest wages, while the surplus wealth generated by these low paid workers is flowing back into the richer countries along with the produced goods to be consumed. And in the case of the US, the surplus wealth flowing into the country is also not distributed back to the population (who are loosing their jobs because of this situation), which is what causes the potential of loosing these big american industries to become a "problem", from a purely american perspective that is. 

Anyway, strong unions with a strong state backing them up is what solves these issues, at least on a national level. It keeps key industries in the country by political intervention, at the same time allowing for innovation and growing productivity by letting unproductive businesses fail, providing for the workers inevitably needing new jobs, while also safe-guarding the lives of the workers, preventing them being exploited in the name of "productivity", which in turn increases productivity in the long term as the workers themselves get an interest in increasing productivity, as that is what drives their wage growth. And so on. On a global level we need to fix the broken system were keeping wages low is essentially encouraged. The labor of an indonesian person is not actually worth like 10 times less than the labor of an equally skilled american, a system that encourages that kind of disparity is clearly broken.

Author: @xeutoniumnyborg1192
Content:
The rot in the American automotive industry has been decades in the making. In the early 1950s, W Edwards Deming approached the Big 3, AMC, and Packard with his ideas for improved manufacturing through quality management and control. All of them basically told Deming to GTFO. Deming took his ideas to Japan, who was still in the process of rebuilding its economy from WWII. Japan's industries, including its car manufacturers, embraced Deming's concepts and its been reflected in their products since.

In 1998, I attended a training seminar on IM240 emissions testing, which was being implemented in Illinois. The instructors showed us a 1981 Toyota Corolla they bought sight unseen from a roadside lot. They repaired the Corrola's emissions systems and exhaust, and it passed the IM240 smog test. I strongly doubt a 1981 Chevy Citation bought in the same manner could match the Corrola's test performance, if the Citation was even road worthy.

Author: @roch145
Content:
US car companies are driven by short term thinking, short term goals and compensation that is driver by stock performance and not other metrics such as market share, profitability, quality and customer satisfaction.  Additionally, US automotive engineers are very different from their German and Japanese counterparts.  US engineers design philosophy is to produce products that are good enough for the task at hand with no real emphasis on superior design and performance.  This creates real shortcomings in product design, longevity and reliability.  US engineers don’t “sweat the details” like they did in the past.  Quasi monopoly of the US automotive market prior to 1980 offered very little competitive motivation for quality improvement and reliability in American cars.  Fortunately the Japanese entered the market to give consumers much better choices. 

Don’t underestimate the impact of the UAW on the decline of the US auto industry.  Wages and benefits are high.  Especially compared with Japan and South Korea.  None of the foreign manufacturers building cars in the US employ union labor.  And virtually all of them are located in southern “red” states that offer lower costs, not just labor, but taxes and regulations.  Additionally, UAW labor rules are not flexible, limiting the roles each worker can assume, requiring more headcount due to role restrictions. 

So as much as people want to complain about the greed of corporations as being a problem with the US auto corporations, there’s also the greed of the unions.  

I don’t ever see myself buying “Big Three” manufactured vehicle in the future.  Most of my cars have been Japanese or German.  Though I have bought Fords and GMC’s in the past and have never ever been very impressed with them.

Author: @sasz2107
Content: The Arab oil embargoes of 1973-74 and 1979 is what really changed things in terms of people starting to buy Japanese cars - not emissions and safety concerns. Honda didn't sell any cars until 1974.  Having owned a Toyota from the early 70s, Japanese cars from that time period were practically go karts. They weren't these high quality vehicles the way they are portrayed.  They did improve a lot on subsequent years.  2:30 - the Big 3 DID put a huge focus on smaller more fuel efficient cars!  You totally missed that!  What about all of the downsizing of the Big 3 cars between 1977 and 1985?  How could you leave that out?  You make comments like "they didn't do anything" when they absolutely did! GM changed ALL if their entire car lines to front wheel drive!  Chrysler did the same thing except for the M body Diplomat and Gran Fury during the 80s.  However, they can't make as much profit off small cars as the Japanese can because the Big 3 had massive overhead costs - e.g. VERY generous employee retirement packages - including pensions and lifetime health care for employees AND spouses. They made a bigger profit off of trucks.  The ever increasing fuel mileage regulations (CAFE) was stricter for cars than for trucks.  It was easier for them to create the luxury SUV market (which barely existed except for Jeeps before the early 1990s) that didn't have to meet the same fuel economy standards.  They moved away form traditional full sized cars with body on frame construction and over to trucks/SUVs.  You can't tow a trailer or a boat with a front wheel drive unibody car with a V6 engine that's called "full sized".  And look - today, people STILL buy LOTS of truck based SUVs.  No one could have predicted the oil crises of 1973 and 1979, or the massive increase in the price of oil starting around 2005, or the recession created by the subprime mortgage crisis in 2008.  So my point is, if they can't make a profit off of small cars but they CAN make a profit off of trucks to cover all of their massive overhead costs, and because government fuel economy regulations pushed things this way, why would they NOT move over to SUVs?  Even if it hurt them in the end?  What else were they supposed to do?  You can criticize them and act like they are idiots, but you know, sometimes circumstances come against people or against businesses that are outside their control that they can't do anything about.  e.g. What about the railroads in the mid 20th century?  Circumstances came against them and many of them went out of business.  Sound familiar?

Author: @k-nickDTX
Content:
Worked for a rental car company for a few years in the 2010s. Ford and FCA's sedans were TRASH. The epitome of a mailed-in, bare-minimum effort product from a dying company committed to shaving every possible penny off production costs. Not only did they look and feel cheaply made, but they were incredibly unreliable. Our Ford Fusions sat on the lot for months because we couldn't rent them due to a major recall in the steering column... which Ford couldn't fix because of a months-long parts backlog. The Focus and Fiesta's transmissions were so bad the entire car would lurch and shake violently every time they started rolling from stop or shifted gears at lower speeds. We'd have customers come back all the time complaining that the car was about to break underneath them. And, sure enough, sometimes that rough shifting would cause the transmissions to tear themselves apart, sometimes in as little as 20k miles or less. Even the absolute cheapest Hyundai Accent, performed better and was more reliable.

Customers also complained a lot about the Chrysler 200's gear shifter knob looking like a volume knob causing them to put the car into neutral (or even reverse) while driving down the freeway at speed. Breathtakingly bad design.

Author: @htklun
Content:
The Japanese pioneered a term called Galápagos syndrome, which describes the insular Japanese electronics industry catering to protected domestic markets to the point that their technology evolved to such an extent that they have no viable market outside of their home.  This is true of the US auto industry too.  The Chicken tax and policy of cheap oil skewed the American auto market to such an extent Ford and GM really don't know how to build anything but trucks / SUVs.  

Looking into the future, I don't see a viable way for the Big 2.5 - Stellantis is for all intents and purposes FIAT - to compete and turn a profit when even European and Japanese legacy car makers are panicking over the rise of the Chinese EV industry.  BYD is gaining massive market share in South East Asia and Latin America largely at the expense of Toyota, and Honda, while in Europe BYD is selling cars with luxury amenities and features comparable to luxury or super luxury brands but at a fraction of the price.  Even Tesla is losing sales in head to head competition against BYD, and there are probably another 4~5 Chinese EV brands itching it expand in Europe.  The only reason Ford and GM are still clinging on is because of the 130% EV tariffs (100% from Biden, another 30% from Trump... for now).   As long as these tariffs are in place, American auto will continue to be a Galápagos, and US consumers will have fewer choices.

Author: @ObeseChess
Content:
I posted this on Regular Car Reviews' review of the 2015 Ford Fiesta Titanium, but it applies to this video, too (I've made a few adjustments to the text before pasting):

[The 2015 Fiesta Titanium] is a great illustration of how Ford does business, and all of this is me speaking from experience.

As noted in the review, the Titanium was slotted below the ST - the Titanium fully optioned was just under $20k, whereas a fully-loaded ST cost just under $30k. However, the Titanium has a number of features that the ST did not get, such as rear parking sensors, a backup camera, an auto-dimming compass mirror, and a few other things. Despite this, the "Titanium" parts are not plug-and-play with the ST, as the cars use COMPLETELY different wiring harnesses. So, for example, if you want the auto-dimming compass mirror (which was advertised as standard on the ST, but was not actually included) you have to solder in a bunch of wires, despite the headliners being the same to the point that there are channels through which to run those wires. Same with the backup camera - you can buy the harness from the dealership and retrofit it, but it wasn't included on the car that cost $10,000 more. Rear parking sensors, nobody's been able to get those to work yet.

This is also true of the interior switchgear, which is different between the S, SE, Titanium, and ST. The switches are all PHYSICALLY identical outside of having a different color backlight, but they are not plug and play as each is completely different INSIDE despite having the same FUNCTION. So let's say your dashboard dimmer switch in your ST goes out, or you want to change your interior lighting color from teal to red, so you grab a dimmer switch from an SE at a junkyard. The switch physically plugs right in, and then the dashboard lights turn COMPLETELY off. SE or ST window switches in a Titanium will cause the windows to roll down all the way and not roll back up. S, SE, or Titanium charging ports don't work with the ST head unit. Absolutely NOTHING is plug-and-play across multiple cars of the same model year with identical chassis. 

Oh, and this is only true of the US models. The Fiesta STs sold in the rest of the world had COMPLETELY different interiors with their own sets of switchgear (radios, steering wheels, airbags, climate control, center consoles, shift knobs and boots, ambient lighting, etc are all completely different in the US) which are also not plug and play. So EVERY SINGLE PART on this car has between four and eight different SKUs depending on trim and region, NONE of them are interchangeable, and NONE of them are shared with anything else in the Ford lineup.

No wonder Ford wasn't making money on these things.

Author: @JonoSSD
Content:
Ford manufactured vehicles in Brazil for literally 100 years. The Brazilian branch was even more profitable than the US one between 2003 and 2014. Yet, in 2021 the company closed all its local factories and essentially left the country, only selling a few very expensive imported models since then. It alleged a difficult economic scenario even though it was in the top 5 most sold brands back then. And Brazil being one of the largest car markets in the entire world (oscillating between #6 and #8 in the past years), while also having record car sales in the past few years. Every single number points to a great scenario. It makes no sense for Ford to ignore such a lucrative market. 

Meanwhile, Chinese brands have been quickly dominating sales and streets, with billions being invested to advertise and even starting to manufacture their cards here. Soon, most cars sold in Brazil will be Chinese and even though these brands have been investing heavily on our market, other car manufactures are also to blame for being so slow to adapt to this new influx of competitors. As someone who has worked in advertising for motor companies, especially Japanese ones, I can say it's definitely not just Ford or GM. Honda, Nissan and Toyota have also been slow on the uptake. It was honestly frustrating presenting so much data, explaining the threat and what they could do about it only to be brushed off by old execs who haven't used a computer past Windows 95 and think advertising on radio and TV (and very little, might I add) is their best bet at this point. Japanese brands still carry a lot of weight here, but that is fading and fast. Mitsubishi and Suzuki, for example, once names everyone knew, are all but dead. BYD, GWM, Chery are in for no reason other than they are doing what the others could but aren't. Their cars aren't better, they're just advertised exponentially better. Other segments like home appliances, once dominated by the likes of Panasonic, Sharp, etc, now are all Chinese. Even more "modern" dominating brands like LG or Samsung are starting to feel the heat. And sure, this is happening everywhere, but here is in turbo mode, right now especially in vehicles. 

For anyone curious, search "FENABRAVE emplacamentos", which is essentially a monthly census of all new cars sold in Brazil. By brand and segment. You can see Chinese brands gaining ground every year while almost everyone else shrinks. And most of these Chinese brands haven't been here long at all.

If anyone wants videos that go more in-depth on the American car industry's troubles watch Regular Car Reviews' videos on the subject. They are extremely well-researched. But on this video's topic the main reason a lot of public American companies suck regardless of industry is the Friedman doctrine. Friedman described it as: “There is one and only one social responsibility of business..to use its resources and engage in activities designed to increase its profits so long as it . . . engages in open and free competition without deception or fraud.” 

Of course American companies (and honestly a huge issue with corporatism itself) will want to snuff out competition or have too few. It's common to have 3 companies really only feel like one cause they will not compete enough with each other, price fix, or any other sort of issue. A great example of this is the insulin industry. Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, and Sanofi. They tend to price fix insulin and while it definitely makes them a profit they are beyond evil for doing so. There needs to be leas of a focus on making as much profit as possible and more on long-term business strategies. I would not be opposed to abolishing the stock market but I doubt it's a realistic solution. Taking these companies private is most likely the better solution since they won't feel obligated to shareholders and can make better decisions. Usually the best American companies are private for a reason. Anyways, that's enough economics ranting on my end.

Content:
You didn’t mention a key piece of history that got these auto manufacturers to shift to big vehicles. That was the book “Unsafe at Any Speed,” which denounced the Chevy Corvair. That car was their attempt in the early 1960s to put a heavy focus on the small car market - away from cars that rely on big engines (and burn a lot of fuel). But people came to the conclusion that these cars were dangerous, so GM shifted focus to larger cars - and largely stayed there. Largely. There was another big push to get into the compact market a decade later, when the Chevy Vega was introduced in 1971 - two years before the gas crisis. Author: @SmallPrintBigProblems
Content:
The downfall of many iconic brands—especially in the auto industry—can be traced to a single destructive ideology: the shareholder-first mindset.

American companies are obsessed with maximising short-term returns for shareholders, often at the expense of product quality, brand integrity, and long-term vision. This isn’t just a business strategy; it’s a cultural doctrine embedded in universities, corporate boardrooms, media, and government policy.

Take Ford, for example. It once owned Jaguar, Land Rover, and Aston Martin—brands rich in heritage, design philosophy, and loyal customer bases. But rather than investing in what made these marques special, Ford treated them like units on a spreadsheet. The focus wasn’t on building world-class cars—it was on cutting costs, consolidating platforms, and improving quarterly results.

Jaguar, in particular, had the potential to take on BMW’s performance while offering Mercedes-level luxury. Instead, it was saddled with generic Ford platforms, resulting in vehicles that were underwhelming to drive, unreliable, and completely outclassed by their European rivals. The cars were engineered for financial efficiency—not emotional connection or market differentiation.

But this isn’t just about Ford. It’s a systemic issue across American capitalism. The pro-shareholder model treats a company like a chicken whose only purpose is to lay as many eggs as possible. So, they push the chicken harder—less feed, smaller cages, fewer rest days. When the chicken inevitably gets sick or dies, they don’t rethink the system. They blame the chicken, lay off other chickens, slash wages, and tighten controls even further.

Then they look around, bewildered that egg quality is declining, and point fingers at foreign chickens, regulation, or the market—anything but their own ideology.

Until this mindset changes, no brand—no matter how iconic—is safe. Companies will continue to devour their own potential in pursuit of short-term gains, only to wonder why they’re left with hollowed-out shells where great legacies used to be.

Author: @porthose2002
Content: Boy, Sam.  Wendover Productions is on my "Must Watch" list and I love your work, but IMO this episode is missing much of the well thought through logic of other videos you've released.  It's certainly been accepted as fact that the Japanese manufacturers have made the most generally reliable vehicles since the 1970's.  That's not new.  So trying to make the claim that buyers are buying larger vehicles from the Big Three simply because they are marketing them to us that way, or because Ford decided to no longer make cars, just doesn't work logically for me.  First off, all the manufacturers market to us, regardless of their countries of origin, so they have as much influence (and skin in the game) as the American companies do.  Second, the same trend towards light trucks and SUVs is occurring across brands.  For instance, the Honda Civic (with an MSRP of abt. 24K) sold 242K vehicles in 2024, yet the CR-V (MSRP of over 30K) sold 4043K.  The CR-V is vastly more profitable for Honda than the Civic is and these two vehicles are built on the same frame.  So while you may be able to assert that the American auto manufacturers benefit, so do the others.  Lastly, yes we Americans can be a gullible lot, but more often than not, if you build a better mousetrap with a compelling reason to adopt (Betamax not withstanding) the market and the buying public will react.

Author: @jlcii
Content:
I personally have a preference for a truck or an SUV. While I might consider a car as a secondary vehicle for occasions, I couldn't imagine having my daily driver be an uncomfortable car with a low roof line and lack of interior room. I'm a tall girl, and I like my space and versatility. So I do understand why SUVs and crossovers have taken off in sales. 

To each their own on what people like, but a lot of people that have families or simply want space, utility, and prioritize safety typically aren't going to seek out sports cars and small cars to be their main vehicles. Have you tried fitting a stroller into the trunk of a Dodge Challenger? And go ahead and try to go grocery shopping at Costco in a hot hatch. And as a regular road trip driver personally, a RAV4 is a lot more comfortable to spend 5 plus hours in than a Corolla. 

Contrary to this belief that people are somehow coerced into buying SUVs and pickups, most people given the choice would not choose a car over an SUV/Truck. They're likely not going to choose the less comfortable and less safe vehicle over the more comfortable and more safe vehicle. I think auto enthusiasts aren't necessarily realistic when it comes to their perspectives about the automotive market. Just because you want a Supra, a Challenger, or a Civic Type R doesn't mean 500,000 other people do.

Author: @dmac7128
Content:
The autoworker unions are scapegoated unfairly in reference to the failures of the US auto industry.  Yes, labor costs are among the highest in the industry.  But so are executive overhead costs.  The pay gap between executives and employees in US auto companies is considerably higher than the gap within the Japanese and European automakers.   
The problem comes down to several points.  The US auto industry between 1945 and 1975 had no competition.  The chicken tax  tariff in 1965 effectively shielded Detroit from any competition in the light truck sector for over 25 years until foreign trucks started to be made in the US.  With a built in 25 percent markup on all foreign trucks, that allowed Detroit to operate on fat profit margins on every truck sold.  Compound that with the CAFE standards of the 70s that gave Detroit every incentive to pour most of their R&D, advertising, quality control into light trucks.  And making sh!tty cars was a feature, not a bug.  It made it that much easier to upsell gullible Americans on the "virtues" of these pavement queens at a considerably higher profit margin.

Author: @classiclibertarian
Content:
American cars got so bad because: 

1. Unions (with government granted monopoly in the form of "closed shop") - Mainly in the form of driving up costs and decreasing the ROI of investments in new plant and equipment in locations where synergies existed (midwest). This lack of investment and cost advantage lowered its ability to innovate. This trend is slowing somewhat as auto manufacturers relocated to right-to-work (non-union) states, but these locations are otherwise not ideal from a logistical point of view.
2. Fuel efficiency regulations - Increased mandates for fuel efficiency meant that US firms, already overburdened by unions, now faced additional costs in making their cars more fuel efficient. combined with the fact that tariffs were no high enough on foreign cars, this meant hemorrhaging business to foreign firms. As explained in the video, this also resulted in a focus on trucks, where the US actually unquestionably dominates (particularly large trucks).
3. Foreign tariffs - Foreign countries, particularly with large markets, have long had high tariffs and non-tariff barriers on US manufactured goods (Higher than what the US imposes on them), and in particular on US automobiles. This has resulted in a competitive disadvantage for US producers in that foreign competitors can benefit from additional scale (selling to both their domestic market and the large US market) while US firms can really only compete in the American market competitively.
